title: Preparing a Five-Minute Teaching Demo
script: Nisa: [thoughtful] Mr. Adnan, my teaching interview includes a five-minute lesson. I have planned twelve slides.
Mr. Adnan: Twelve slides in five minutes may leave no time for learners to think. What is your single learning goal?
Nisa: [reflective] I want them to identify three signs of a reliable online source.
Mr. Adnan: That is clear. Can they practice the skill during the lesson?
Nisa: [honestly] I planned to explain all three signs and show many examples.
Mr. Adnan: Choose one short example first. Ask learners what they notice before you explain.
Nisa: [encouraged] So the first minute could show two websites with different authors and dates.
Mr. Adnan: Yes. Then collect two observations, introduce the three signs, and let them check one new example.
Nisa: [determined] I am worried silence will make me look unprepared.
Mr. Adnan: A brief thinking pause shows that you expect learners to participate. Tell them they have ten seconds.
Nisa: [warmly] How should I end the demo?
Mr. Adnan: Ask one final question that reveals whether they can use the idea, not whether they remember your definition.
Nisa: [hopeful] Perhaps: “Which source would you open first, and what would you check?”
Mr. Adnan: Good. Their reason matters more than choosing the picture you prefer.
Nisa: [gently] Do I need printed materials?
Mr. Adnan: One half-page example is enough. Bring a backup in case the screen does not work.
Nisa: I will reduce the slides to four: goal, comparison, three signs, and final task.
Mr. Adnan: [warmly] Practice with a timer, including the pause and one possible student answer.
Nisa: What if the interviewer gives no answer?
Mr. Adnan: Say what a learner might notice and continue calmly. Do not turn the demo into a rushed speech.
Nisa: I understand. Five minutes should show one complete learning moment, not a whole course.

quiz.question: How many slides did Nisa first plan?
quiz.explanation: Her first plan was too crowded for five minutes.

quiz.question: What is the learning goal?
options: Identify three signs of a reliable online source
quiz.explanation: The lesson has one specific digital-literacy goal.

quiz.question: Why include ten seconds of silence?
quiz.explanation: A stated pause supports active thinking.

quiz.question: What backup should she bring?
quiz.explanation: A small printout protects the core activity.

quiz.question: What should the demo show?
quiz.explanation: Depth and learner action matter more than coverage.

quiz.question: Why are twelve slides a problem beyond speed?
options: The interview allows only four colors
They leave little space for learner thinking and practice
The screen cannot show twelve files
quiz.explanation: Teaching quality is not the amount of content displayed.

quiz.question: What makes the first comparison active?
options: Learners observe two sites before receiving the explanation

quiz.question: Why announce a ten-second pause?
options: Learners understand that silence is intentional thinking time
quiz.explanation: Clear timing prevents silence from feeling accidental.

quiz.question: What does the final question assess?
options: Whether learners can apply checks to a source
Whether they can read twelve slides
quiz.explanation: A reasoned choice reveals usable understanding.

quiz.question: How should Nisa handle no audience answer?
options: Model a possible observation and continue calmly
Wait for the whole five minutes
quiz.explanation: The demo remains interactive in design without depending on a real class response.
